# **Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data**

## **Learning Outcome**

By the end of this hands-on exercise this exercise will be able create the followings data visualisation by using R packages:

- plotting a calender heatmap by using ggplot2 functions,

- plotting a cycle plot by using ggplot2 function,

- plotting a slopegraph

- plotting a horizon chart


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes,
               gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table,
               CGPfunctions, ggHoriPlot, tidyverse)
```
:::


## **1. Plotting Calendar Heatmap**

In this section, a calendar heatmap will be plotted programmatically by using ggplot2 package.

![](https://r4va.netlify.app/chap17/img/image01.png)

By the end of this section, I will be able to:

- plot a calender heatmap by using ggplot2 functions and extension,

- to write function using R programming,

- to derive specific date and time related field by using base R and lubridate packages

- to perform data preparation task by using tidyr and dplyr packages.

### **1.1 The Data**

For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, *eventlog.csv* file will be used. This data file consists of 199,999 rows of time-series cyber attack records by country.

### **1.2 Importing the data**

First, use the code chunk below to import *eventlog.csv* file into R environment and called the data frame as *attacks*.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
attacks <- read.csv("data/eventlog.csv")
```
:::


### **1.3 Examining the data structure**

It is always a good practice to examine the imported data frame before further analysis is performed.

For example, *kable()* can be used to review the structure of the imported data frame.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
kable(head(attacks))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|timestamp                   |source_country |tz              |
|:---------------------------|:--------------|:---------------|
|2015-03-12T15:59:16.718901Z |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |
|2015-03-12T16:00:48.841746Z |FR             |Europe/Paris    |
|2015-03-12T16:02:26.731256Z |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |
|2015-03-12T16:02:38.469907Z |US             |America/Chicago |
|2015-03-12T16:03:22.201903Z |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |
|2015-03-12T16:03:45.984616Z |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |


:::
:::


There are three columns, namely *timestamp*, *source_country* and *tz*.

- *timestamp* field stores date-time values in POSIXct format.

- *source_country* field stores the source of the attack. It is in *ISO 3166-1 alpha-2* country code.

- *tz* field stores time zone of the source IP address.

### **1.4 Data Preparation**

Step 1: Deriving *weekday* and *hour of day* fields

Before we can plot the calender heatmap, two new fields namely *wkday* and *hour* need to be derived. In this step, we will write a function to perform the task.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts,
                        tz = tz[1],
                        quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)                 
  }
```
:::


::: callout-note
Take Note

- [`ymd_hms()`](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/reference/ymd_hms.html) and [`hour()`](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/reference/hour.html) are from [**lubridate**](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/) package, and

- [`weekdays()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/base/versions/3.6.2/topics/weekdays) is a **base** R function.
:::

Step 2: Deriving the attacks tibble data frame


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday',
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday',
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday',
                  'Sunday')

attacks <-  attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp,
                   .$source_country,
                   .$tz)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(wkday = factor(
    wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour = factor(
      hour, levels = 0:23))
```
:::


::: callout-note
## Take Note

Beside extracting the necessary data into *attacks* data frame, `mutate()` of **dplyr** package is used to convert *wkday* and *hour* fields into **factor** so they’ll be ordered when plotting
:::

Table below shows the tidy tibble table after processing.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
kable(head(attacks))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|tz           |source_country |wkday    |hour |
|:------------|:--------------|:--------|:----|
|Africa/Cairo |BG             |Saturday |22   |
|Africa/Cairo |TW             |Sunday   |8    |
|Africa/Cairo |TW             |Sunday   |10   |
|Africa/Cairo |CN             |Sunday   |13   |
|Africa/Cairo |US             |Sunday   |17   |
|Africa/Cairo |CA             |Monday   |13   |


:::
:::


### **2 Building the Calendar Heatmaps**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
grouped <- attacks %>%
  count(wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

ggplot(grouped,
       aes(hour,
           wkday,
           fill = n)) +
geom_tile(color = "white",
            size = 0.1) +
theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
coord_equal() +
scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue",
                    high = "dark blue") +
labs(x = NULL,
       y = NULL,
       title = "Attacks by weekday & time of day") +
theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: callout-note
## Learning from Above Code Chunk

- a tibble data table called *grouped* is derived by aggregating the attack by *wkday* and *hour* fields.

- a new field called *n* is derived by using `group_by()` and `count()` functions.

- `na.omit()` is used to exclude missing value.

- `geom_tile()` is used to plot tiles (grids) at each x and y position. `color` and `size` arguments are used to specify the border color and line size of the tiles.

- `coord_equal()` is used to ensure the plot will have an aspect ratio of 1:1.

- `scale_fill_gradient()` function is used to creates a two colour gradient (low-high).
:::

Then we can simply group the count by hour and wkday and plot it, since we know that we have values for every combination there’s no need to further preprocess the data.

### **2.1 Building Multiple Calendar Heatmaps**

**Challenge:** Building multiple heatmaps for the top four countries with the highest number of attacks.

![](https://r4va.netlify.app/chap17/img/image02.png)

### **2.2 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps**

Step 1: Deriving attack by country object

In order to identify the top 4 countries with the highest number of attacks, it is required to do the followings:

- count the number of attacks by country,

- calculate the percent of attackes by country, and

- save the results in a tibble data frame.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
attacks_by_country <- count(
  attacks, source_country) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n/sum(n))) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
```
:::


Step 2: Preparing the tidy data frame

In this step, it is required to extract the attack records of the top 4 countries from *attacks* data frame and save the data in a new tibble data frame (i.e. *top4_attacks*).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
top4 <- attacks_by_country$source_country[1:4]
top4_attacks <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top4) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(source_country = factor(
    source_country, levels = top4)) %>% 
  na.omit()
```
:::


### **2.3 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps**

Step 3: Plotting the Multiple Calender Heatmap by using ggplot2 package.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
ggplot(top4_attacks,
       aes(hour,
           wkday,
           fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white",
             size = 0.1) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                      low = "sky blue",
                      high = "dark blue") +
  facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x=NULL, y=NULL,
       title = "Attacks on top 4 countries by weekday & time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## **3 Plotting Cycle Plot**

In this section, a cycle plot showing the time-series patterns and trend of visitor arrivals from Vietnam programmatically by using ggplot2 functions.

![](https://r4va.netlify.app/chap17/img/image03.png)

### **3.1 Step 1: Data Import**

For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, *arrivals_by_air.xlsx* will be used.

The code chunk below imports *arrivals_by_air.xlsx* by using `read_excel()` of **readxl** package and save it as a tibble data frame called *air*.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
air <- read_excel("data/arrivals_by_air.xlsx")
```
:::


### **3.2 Step 2: Deriving month and year fields**

Next, two new fields called *month* and *year* are derived from *Month-Year* field.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
air$month <- factor(month(air$'Month-Year'),
                    level = 1:12,
                    labels = month.abb,
                    ordered = TRUE)
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))
```
:::


### **3.3 Step 3: Extracting the target country**

Next, the code chunk below is use to extract data for the target country (i.e. Vietnam)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
Vietnam <-air %>%
  select('Vietnam',
         month,
         year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)
```
:::


### **3.4 Step 4: Computing year average arrivals by month**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
hline.data <- Vietnam %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(Vietnam, na.rm = TRUE))
```
:::


### **3.5 Step 5: Plotting the cycle plot**

The code chunk below is used to plot the cycle plot as shown in Slide 12/23.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = Vietnam,
            aes(x = year,
                y = Vietnam,       # Removed quotation marks here
                group = month),
            colour = "black") +
  geom_hline(data = hline.data,
             aes(yintercept = avgvalue),
             linetype = 6,
             colour = "red",
             linewidth = 1) +    # Changed 'size' to 'linewidth'
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(title = "Visitors Arrival from Vietnam via Air, Jan 2010 - Dec 2019",
       x = "",
       y = "No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Arial") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),   # Moved axis formatting into theme()
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank())  # Added this to remove the tick marks as well
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## **4 Plotting Slopegraph**

Before getting start, make sure that **CGPfunctions** has been installed and loaded onto R environment. Then, refer to [Using newggslopegraph](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/CGPfunctions/vignettes/Using-newggslopegraph.html) to learn more about the function. Lastly, read more about `newggslopegraph()` and its arguments by referring to this [link](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/CGPfunctions/versions/0.6.3/topics/newggslopegraph).

### **4.1 Step 1: Data Import**

Import the rice data set into R environment by using the code chunk below.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
rice <- read_csv("data/rice.csv")
```
:::


### **4.2 Step 2: Plotting the slopegraph**

Due to an error where the needed packages cannot be installed.![](images/clipboard-2676231804.png)

The code chunk below will us tidyverse and ggrepel instead of slopegraph as shown below.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Display Code"}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)

# 1. Filter the data just like before
df_slope <- rice %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(1961, 1980)) %>%
  mutate(Year = factor(Year)) # Ensure Year is treated as a category for the X-axis

# 2. Build the plot
ggplot(df_slope, aes(x = Year, y = Yield, group = Country, color = Country)) +
  # Draw the connecting lines
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.8) +
  
  # Add points at each end
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  
  # Add left-side labels (1961) - ggrepel will prevent overlapping!
  geom_text_repel(data = df_slope %>% filter(Year == "1961"), 
                  aes(label = paste(Country, Yield)), 
                  hjust = 1, 
                  nudge_x = -0.1, # Push slightly left of the point
                  direction = "y") + # Only shift text up/down to avoid overlap
  
  # Add right-side labels (1980)
  geom_text_repel(data = df_slope %>% filter(Year == "1980"), 
                  aes(label = paste(Yield, Country)), 
                  hjust = 0, 
                  nudge_x = 0.1, # Push slightly right of the point
                  direction = "y") +
  
  # Formatting to make it look like the CGPfunctions version
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none", # Hide the side legend since we labeled the lines directly
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), # Remove vertical grid lines
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  labs(title = "Rice Yield of Top 11 Asian Countries",
       subtitle = "1961-1980",
       x = NULL, # Hide the "Year" x-axis label for a cleaner look
       y = "Yield",
       caption = "Prepared by Joshua")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: callout-note
## Learning from Above Code Chunk

For effective data visualisation design, `factor()` is used convert the value type of *Year* field from numeric to factor.
:::
